text: Compliance of pedestrian infrastructure with accessibility standards is rarely verified at city scale because manual slope measurement is slow and inconsistent. We deployed a vehicle-mounted mobile laser scanner across 84 km of urban streets and developed a segmentation routine that isolates sidewalk surfaces from the resulting point cloud. Longitudinal grade, cross slope and clear width were computed at one-metre intervals and compared against regulatory thresholds. Validation against manual inclinometer readings on 120 reference segments showed mean absolute errors below 0.4 percent. Point-cloud quality control removed transient objects and poorly registered sections; 183 reference locations were retained for geometric validation. A separate sensitivity analysis of automated extraction of sidewalk longitudinal and cross slope from mobile laser scanning was conducted on 106 observations using a different parameterisation. An additional extraction of sidewalk longitudinal and cross slope from mobile laser scanning analysis used a separate subset of 71 records to assess sensitivity to analytical choices. A supplementary check of automated extraction of sidewalk longitudinal and cross slope from mobile laser scanning used 48 records selected independently from the primary analytical sample. The resulting inventory identified 3,100 non-compliant segments concentrated in older districts.

text: Curb ramps are a prerequisite for barrier-free pedestrian travel, yet municipal inventories are frequently incomplete. This study fine-tuned a detection model on 14,000 annotated street-level images to locate curb ramps at intersections and to classify their condition as intact, damaged or absent. The model achieved a mean average precision of 0.81 on a held-out test set. Image quality was screened for severe blur and occlusion before feature extraction, leaving 163 independent locations for reference comparison. To examine analytical stability, 105 observations relevant to detecting missing and damaged curb ramps from street-level imagery using an object detection network were evaluated under an alternative specification. Validation sites were distributed across 11 subareas so that model performance was not assessed only in streets resembling the development sample. Applied to an entire mid-sized city, the pipeline flagged 27 percent of intersections as lacking at least one compliant ramp, and results were verified by field inspection of a stratified sample.

text: Nominal sidewalk width overstates the space actually available to pedestrians because poles, signage, parked vehicles and street furniture reduce the usable corridor. We fused street-level panoramic images with synchronised lidar returns to segment the paved surface and to detect intruding objects. Effective width was then computed as the largest obstruction-free corridor at each location. Point-cloud quality control removed transient objects and poorly registered sections; 78 reference locations were retained for geometric validation. Across a downtown study area, effective width was on average 0.9 m narrower than the cadastral value, and 18 percent of segments fell below the minimum required for two-way pedestrian flow.

text: Surface irregularity is a determinant of comfort and safety for pedestrians and a barrier for wheelchair users, but it is seldom mapped systematically. Volunteers carried instrumented smartphones and wheelchair-mounted accelerometers along 60 km of routes, and vertical acceleration signals were converted into a roughness index calibrated against a reference profilometer. Spatially aggregated results revealed systematic differences between central and peripheral districts, and the index correlated with participants' self-reported discomfort ratings collected immediately after each trip. text: Pedestrian network datasets are absent or incomplete in most cities, which limits routing and equity analysis. We applied a semantic segmentation model to 210,000 street-level images to detect sidewalk presence on each side of every street segment, and reconstructed a topologically connected pedestrian network. text: Distance-based accessibility measures ignore vertical effort, which is decisive in topographically complex cities. text: Safe crossing opportunities are a central component of the pedestrian environment but are rarely inventoried at scale. text: Pedestrian comfort and safety depend on proximity and speed of adjacent motor traffic. Roadside radar units recorded vehicle speeds and volumes at 42 street segments while street imagery was segmented to measure carriageway width, buffer presence and parking configuration. text: Static weather stations poorly represent the thermal conditions experienced while walking. Instrumented carts and body-worn sensors recorded air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and globe temperature along repeated walking transects during summer afternoons. text: Shade is a decisive determinant of walking comfort in hot climates, yet canopy cover measured from above does not indicate whether the walking surface itself is shaded. This work combined mobile lidar point clouds with hemispherical images captured at pedestrian height to reconstruct sky view factor and to simulate shadow projection onto the sidewalk across the day. Segment-level shade duration was validated against on-site pyranometer readings. text: Air quality shapes the healthfulness of walking but is usually inferred from sparse regulatory monitors. text: Noise is a recognised component of pedestrian comfort yet is rarely incorporated in walkability assessment. Calibrated sound level meters were carried along pedestrian routes while synchronised imagery was segmented to describe facade continuity, vegetation and street width. text: Radiant heat from paving contributes to discomfort during summer walking but is not captured by air temperature alone. text: Background: Physical inactivity remains a major risk factor for chronic disease. This cohort study examined whether residential neighbourhood walkability is associated with objectively measured physical activity. Methods: Participants wore hip-mounted accelerometers for seven consecutive days, and moderate-to-vigorous activity was derived using established cut-points. Walkability was assigned from a published composite index combining residential density, intersection density and land use mix at the census tract level. Neighbourhood exposure was assigned within residential or activity-space buffers ranging from 402 to 1106 m in sensitivity analyses. Results: Objective wearable measures, where available, described individual behaviour or health outcomes rather than the physical condition of specific street segments. As a robustness check, 101 observations contributing to neighbourhood walkability and accelerometer-measured physical activity in a cohort of middle-aged adults were analysed with an alternative specification. Robustness of the neighbourhood walkability and accelerometer-measured physical activity in a cohort of middle-aged adults result was examined in 102 observations after changing one preprocessing or modelling assumption. An alternative analysis involving 82 observations was used to assess the stability of the neighbourhood walkability and accelerometer-measured physical activity in a cohort of middle-aged adults finding. Conclusions: Objective wearable measures, where available, described individual behaviour or health outcomes rather than the physical condition of specific street segments. After adjustment for age, sex, income and education, participants in the highest walkability quartile accumulated significantly more daily activity minutes.

text: Understanding cyclist route preferences supports infrastructure planning.
